course.title: Policy Evaluation Lab
course.details: Master's degree (LM) · ECON-02/A · 60 hours · 9 CFU · first semester · taught in English
course.office_hours: By appointment via e-mail (day and time to be confirmed)
course.timetable: Monday, Thursday and Friday, 5:00–7:00 pm · Room 20, Department of Business Economics (Economia Aziendale)

announcements.title: How the course is organised
announcements.body: We study policy evaluation through three lenses: firms as targets of public policy (why governments support or regulate firms, and with which instruments), counterfactual evaluation (the methods: experiments, matching, difference-in-differences, instrumental variables, regression discontinuity, synthetic control), and firms as evaluators of their own decisions (pilots, rollouts and A/B tests). Each method is paired with a reference paper, most of them on Italian incentives to firms: you find them in the week where they are discussed and under Resources.

announcements.title: Welcome to the Policy Evaluation Lab
announcements.body: Slides, datasets, exercises and exam information are posted here. Slides go up before each lecture; datasets and exercises after it. Bring a laptop to the lab sessions.

weeks.summary: Descriptive analysis versus causal inference; potential outcomes, the counterfactual and selection bias. The three lenses of the course: firms as targets of policy, counterfactual evaluation, firms as evaluators of their own decisions. Software set-up.

weeks.topic: Why governments intervene, and regression as a first tool
weeks.summary: Lens 1, firms as targets of policy. Market failures that justify support to firms (externalities, R&D spillovers, credit constraints); the instruments that reach firms in Italy and the EU (investment grants such as Law 488/1992, R&D incentives, tax credits, public guarantees, PNRR). Then the first tool: OLS as a comparison of means, control variables, omitted-variable bias; robust and clustered standard errors.

Why randomisation solves selection bias; balance checks, compliance, intention-to-treat; power and sample size. Lens 3, firms as evaluators: pilots and A/B tests inside companies. Case study: a randomised management-consulting experiment in Indian textile plants (Bloom et al.).

items.label: Bloom, Eifert, Mahajan, McKenzie and Roberts — Does management matter? Evidence from India (NBER WP 16658, 2011; QJE 2013)

weeks.summary: Conditional independence, matching, the propensity score and inverse probability weighting. Application: why firms that apply for a subsidy differ from those that do not, and what matching can and cannot fix.

The 2×2 design, parallel trends, regression formulation. Lab: Card and Krueger on the New Jersey minimum wage. Firm subsidies: Law 488/1992, comparing subsidised firms with rejected applicants, and whether the subsidy created new investment or only moved it in time.

items.label: Card and Krueger — Minimum wages and employment: fast food in New Jersey and Pennsylvania (NBER WP 4509, 1993; AER 1994)
Bronzini and de Blasio — Evaluating the impact of investment incentives: the case of Italy's Law 488/1992 (2006, J. Urban Economics)

weeks.summary: Event studies and pre-trends; staggered adoption and the problems of two-way fixed effects. Lens 3: staggered rollouts of a programme across branches, stores or regions, and how to read them correctly.

Relevance and exclusion, 2SLS, weak instruments, LATE. Lab: Angrist and Krueger (1991) on compulsory schooling. Business framing: encouragement designs, when a programme is offered to everyone but only some take it up.

Sharp and fuzzy designs, bandwidth choice, manipulation tests. Firm incentives allocated by a score threshold (R&D grants in Emilia-Romagna) and by an unexpected shortage of public funds (an Italian innovation programme).

items.label: Bronzini and Iachini — Are incentives for R&D effective? Evidence from a regression discontinuity approach (AEJ: Economic Policy, 2014)
de Blasio, Fantino and Pellegrini — Evaluating the impact of innovation incentives: evidence from an unexpected shortage of funds (Banca d'Italia WP 792, 2011)
Further reading: Cerqua and Pellegrini — Do subsidies to private capital boost firms' growth? A multiple RDD approach (J. Public Economics, 2014)

weeks.summary: Building a counterfactual from a donor pool; inference by placebo. Case study: California Proposition 99. Business framing: evaluating a single large decision, such as a market entry or a regional launch, when there is only one treated unit.

weeks.topic: Evidence for decisions, and report presentations
weeks.summary: Reading an evaluation as a manager: what the evidence supports, what it does not, and how to communicate it. Report presentations and exam review.

exercises.title: Interactive practice on EconVis
exercises.description: Guided challenges, detective mode and interpretation quizzes, with the simulated data downloadable as CSV to rerun in R or Excel.

exercises.title: Problem sets
exercises.description: One problem set per method, posted after the corresponding lab. Solutions are released one week later.

exam.intro: A report on a policy intervention of your choice, presented in the last week of the course, followed by an oral exam.

parts.title: Report
parts.description: On a policy intervention of your choice: either an empirical analysis in R with real-world data, or an argument based on explanation and evidence. The policy can be one you assess as successful or unsuccessful; either way, you have to argue your thesis properly, using solid evidence.

parts.title: Presentation
parts.description: You present your report in the last week of the course (week 10).

parts.title: Oral exam
parts.description: Written instead, if the number of students does not allow us to complete the orals on time.
